sections.title: How complex an exercise is
sections.text: A supported machine row moves along a stable path. A single-leg Romanian deadlift asks for balance, trunk control and hip coordination, and a kettlebell swing adds speed and timing. You can be very strong and still be new to one of these skills.

sections.title: Go from predictable to challenging
sections.text: Start with stable positions and slower reps, and learn one new skill at a time. Then make the exercise harder by taking away support, changing leverage, increasing range or adding controlled speed. A progression should keep the movement’s purpose and avoid changing every demand at once.

sections.title: Fatigue changes coordination
sections.text: An exercise you did well early in a session can get shaky after many reps. Do high-skill exercises earlier, rest longer when you need to, and end a set when your balance or control slips. Complex ballistic drills are usually a poor first choice for a tired beginner.

sections.title: Example
sections.text: If you’re learning lunges, you might start with split squats while holding a rail, move on to unsupported reverse lunges, and try walking lunges later. A faster variation isn’t automatically better.

sections.title: Using TrainUp
sections.text: When TrainUp builds your plan, it picks exercises that fit your level and coordination as well as your limitations and equipment.
